newsitem.title: USA: Simpson trial witness says shoe photo may be fake.
newsitem.headline: Simpson trial witness says shoe photo may be fake.

text.p: A defence expert testified on Wednesday at the O.J. Simpson civil trial that a photograph of the former football star wearing the same kind of shoes worn by the killer of his ex-wife and her friend appears to be a fake.

Robert Groden, an expert in photographic analysis who was called by Simpson's attorneys, said there was a "high likelihood of forgery" in the 1993 photo taken at a pro football game in Buffalo, New York.

The picture, which was introduced earlier by the plaintiffs in the wrongful-death civil lawsuit, shows Simpson wearing the same kind of expensive Bruno Magli shoes that left bloody shoeprints near the bodies of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
In testimony last month Simpson denied he ever owned shoes like those in the photo and insisted it had been doctored.

Under questioning by Simpson attorney Dan Leonard, Groden testified on Wednesday that his analysis of the photo showed at least six discrepancies, including problems with colour balance and tone, alignment of the negative on a film strip and evidence of re-touching.
Simpson was acquitted in criminal court in October 1995 after a yearlong murder trial. He is now facing a wrongful-death civil suit brought by the victims' families, who are seeking monetary damages.
Simpson, who testified for three days earlier in the trial, could return to witness stand as early as Friday for questioning by his own attorneys. No court session was planned for Thursday.
Goldman family attorneys on Wednesday asked Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki to bar Groden from testifying, pointing out that he had no college education or training in photograph analysis.

But the judge said Groden, who served as a photographic consultant to a committee investigating the assasinations of President John F. Kennedy and civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., had sufficient experience to testify.
Groden used blow-ups of the picture and a contact sheet to show jurors what he said was a "false edge" to the negative and a different colour balance to the print.

He said close inspection of the photo, taken by a sports photographer, showed evidence of retouching in the area of Simpson's legs. The right leg, he said, showed a "tonal difference" beginning at about the shin area, while the left leg appears to have "S-shaped" retouching.
Earlier on Wednesday, Simpson lead attorney Robert Baker hammered away at police credibility, suggesting that there was a code of silence among officers.
Baker also contended that police investigating the June 12, 1994, murders may have agreed on a version of events after allegations they had planted evidence to frame Simpson.

Baker's questioning prompted several testy exchanges with patrolman Daniel Gonzalez over what he wrote in his official report after the murders, and what a detective attributed to Gonzalez in an interview six months later.
Gonzalez grew increasingly frustrated with Baker's sarcasm and at one point snapped at the lawyer: "Do you understand what I am trying to tell you?"

Pointing out several discrepancies between officer Gonzalez' official report after the murders and an interview the patrolman gave to Detective Ron Phillips in January, 1995, Baker asked Gonzalez if there was a "code of ethics to cover up other police officers?"
"Yes, you get promoted for burning each other," Gonzalez shot back.
